source: van Eemeren and Grootendorst (1984) Speech Acts in Argumentative Discussions
finding: First full statement of the pragma-dialectical model. It treats argumentation as a speech-act exchange aimed at resolving a difference of opinion, and sets rules for a critical discussion. It is the English version of the Dutch Regels voor redelijke discussies.
numbers: Date and title from the Wikipedia article. No empirical data in the book.
limits: Only a secondary page was read, not the book. The 1984 rule set was later revised into the 2004 version.
agent_relevance: Gives a rule list for a two-party exchange. A single agent could use the rules only as a self-check on its own draft arguments.

source: van Eemeren and Grootendorst (1992, 2004) Argumentation, Communication, and Fallacies; A Systematic Theory of Argumentation
finding: Mature theory. Argumentation is a procedure to resolve a difference of opinion on the merits. Four stages: confrontation, opening, argumentation, concluding. Ten rules govern the procedure.
numbers: 4 stages; 10 rules. Rules: freedom, burden of proof, standpoint, relevance, unexpressed premise, starting point, argument scheme, validity, closure, usage.
limits: Wikipedia summary of the rules. Exact rule wording differs between the 1984, 1992 and 2004 editions.
agent_relevance: The ten rules can be turned into a checklist prompt (see a12). The four stages map loosely onto a single-agent loop: state the claim, fix premises, argue, conclude.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2024) Fallacies; section 3.6 on pragma-dialectics
finding: Pragma-dialectics defines a fallacy as any violation of a rule of the discussion procedure. It rejects all three parts of the standard definition: a fallacy need not be an argument, need not be invalid, and need not look valid. Each classic fallacy maps onto a rule (ad baculum breaks the freedom rule, equivocation the usage rule, post hoc the argument scheme rule). It adds new fallacies such as declaring a standpoint sacrosanct.
numbers: Cites van Eemeren and Grootendorst (2004, p.175) for the claim that every rule violation is a fallacy.
limits: Review text, read through a fetch tool that summarised the page. Appearance of validity is dropped as psychological, which later critics dispute.
agent_relevance: A rule-violation view is easier to code-check than an appearance view. A scaffold can ask whether a step breaks a named rule, not whether it seems sound.

source: van Eemeren and Houtlosser (2006) and van Eemeren (2010) Strategic maneuvering
finding: Strategic maneuvering adds rhetoric to the theory. Arguers pursue reasonableness and effectiveness at once. Three aspects: topic selection, audience adaptation, presentational devices. Fallacies are derailments of strategic maneuvering.
numbers: 3 aspects. Van Eemeren (2010, p.198) as cited in the SEP: all derailments of strategic maneuvering are fallacies.
limits: The extension answers the charge that the pure dialectical model ignored persuasion. It is hard to test, because derailment is judged after the fact.
agent_relevance: An agent that tries to win a user over can drift into derailment. This is a reason to keep the agent's goal as correctness, not persuasion.

source: SEP (2024) Fallacies; sections 3.6 and 4.2 on Walton's challenge
finding: Walton argued for several dialogue types (persuasion, inquiry, negotiation) instead of one critical-discussion model. He kept the appearance condition for fallacies and defined a fallacy as a deceptively bad argument that impedes a dialogue.
numbers: Walton (1995, p.255) five-part definition. Oswald and Herman (2020) and Hansen (2023) are cited for why bad arguments look good.
limits: Competing theory, not a test. The dispute is about definitions and is not settled by data.
agent_relevance: The same move can be fine in negotiation and wrong in inquiry. The schema should state which mode a step is in.

source: Boudry, Paglieri and Pigliucci (2015) The Fake, the Flimsy, and the Fallacious: Demarcating Arguments in Real Life
finding: The 'Fallacy Fork': if fallacies are strictly invalid forms they rarely occur in real life; if defined richly enough for real life they no longer discriminate good from bad. The authors say pragma-dialectics does not escape the fork.
numbers: Abstract only. No sample or numbers; a conceptual argument.
limits: Read the abstract only, not the full paper. It is a philosophical critique, not data.
agent_relevance: Warns that a fallacy checklist will either under-flag or over-flag. Compare the over-flagging seen in LLM detectors (a23).

source: van Eemeren, Meuffels and Verburg (2000) The (Un)Reasonableness of Ad Hominem Fallacies, Journal of Language and Social Psychology 19
finding: Ordinary arguers judged discussion moves with ad hominem fallacies as lacking reasonableness, as the theory predicts. Order from least to most reasonable: direct personal attack, then circumstantial attack, then tu quoque. In a scientific discussion the fallacies were judged less reasonable than in a political debate or a domestic discussion.
numbers: Three ad hominem variants by three discussion types (scientific, political, domestic). Sample size and effect sizes not available; paywalled.
limits: Only the abstract (via Crossref) was read. Judgments depended on context, so the rules are not judged identically everywhere.
agent_relevance: Human intuitions broadly match the rules, but severity varies by setting. A checker could weight violations by setting.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2009) Fallacies and Judgments of Reasonableness (Springer Argumentation Library)
finding: Over ten years of experiments test the conventional validity of the ten rules. Lay arguers with no argumentation training judged discussion fragments that held fallacious and non-fallacious moves. Chapters cover ad hominem, the freedom rule, the obligation to defend (two chapters), the argument scheme rule and the concluding rule.
numbers: 9 chapters, pages 1 to 231. Sample sizes, percentages and effect sizes were not available in the pages I could open.
quote: test methodically the intersubjective acceptability of the rules for critical discussion
limits: Paywalled. I read the publisher page and its blurb only. Treat the strength of support as unknown here.
agent_relevance: This is the main empirical support for the rules. Whether lay judgment matches the rules is a human-norm question, not a test of whether rules improve reasoning.

source: Hample (2010) review of van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2009), Argumentation 24
finding: Hample says the programme offers consistent evidence for the conventional validity of the discussion rules, and that the results on how people view dialogical fallacies stand independent of the pragma-dialectical framework.
numbers: Excerpt on the Springer book page. No numbers.
quote: consistent evidence for the conventional validity of the discussion rules
limits: Reviewer excerpt only. The full review may be more qualified.
agent_relevance: Supports using the rules as a rough human-aligned norm, not as proven law.

source: van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels (2012) The disguised abusive ad hominem empirically investigated, Thinking and Reasoning 18
finding: Abusive ad hominem can look reasonable in real settings when it mimics a legitimate critical reaction to authority argumentation. This is strategic maneuvering with direct personal attacks.
numbers: Not opened. Only a one-line machine summary from Semantic Scholar was seen.
limits: The publisher page was blocked (403). Listed because it is the experimental test of strategic maneuvering.
agent_relevance: If disguised attacks pass as reasonable, a rule-based checker needs context, not surface cues.

source: Hornikx (2010) review in Information Design Journal 18(2) of the 2009 book
finding: Calls the book an extremely good example of how experiments can be designed from a normative theory of argumentation, with a large set of well thought out experiments.
numbers: Excerpt on the Springer book page. No numbers.
limits: Excerpt only.
agent_relevance: The design is a template for testing a rule set against human judgment.

source: Zhou, Westerdijk and Islam (2025) Joint Effects of Argumentation Theory, Audio Modality and Data Enrichment on LLM-Based Fallacy Classification
finding: The only paper found that puts the ten pragma-dialectical rules into an LLM prompt. The model first names the most violated rules, then picks one of six fallacy labels. On Qwen-3 8B, the PD prompt scored 53% accuracy without context against 51% for a basic prompt. It did not beat the basic prompt reliably.
numbers: Task: six fallacy types from US presidential debates (MAMKit, 21,716 entries; test set is balanced, per-class recall steps of 5% suggest about 20 per class, inferred). Base prompt accuracy 51%, macro F1 49%. PD prompt accuracy 53%, macro F1 54%. With context: base 49%, PD 49%. PTA prompt 44%.
quote: base prompts often performed as well as or better than versions with added context
limits: Single 8B model, small test set, no confidence intervals, no repeats. A 2-point gap on about 120 items is within noise. Student project.
agent_relevance: Best evidence on putting PD rules in a prompt: a small or null gain. Do not count on the rules alone to raise accuracy.

source: Zhou et al. (2025), same paper: effect of added context and audio emotion tone
finding: Adding debate context or emotion-tone metadata did not help and sometimes hurt. With the PD prompt, accuracy fell from 53% to 49% with context. With the PTA prompt, accuracy fell from 45% to 25% when audio tone was added. Emotional tone pushed the model toward the label Appeal to Emotion.
numbers: PD per-class F1 base: Ad Hominem 73, Slogans 63, Slippery Slope 50, Appeal to Authority 49, False Cause 45, Appeal to Emotion 44. PTA with audio: macro F1 25%.
limits: Same small-scale limits. The authors admit mapping PD rules onto six labels adds ambiguity.
agent_relevance: Extra context can dilute the check. Keep a rule-check prompt short.

source: Zhou et al. (2025), same paper: Periodic Table of Arguments (Wagemans) vs PD prompt
finding: A structure-based prompt (form, substance, lever) was about as good as the PD prompt without added context and much worse when audio tone was added. Qualitatively PTA did better on appeal to authority; PD did better on ad hominem.
numbers: PTA accuracy: base 44%, context 45%, context plus audio 25%. PTA Ad Hominem F1: 33% base, 62% with context. Slippery Slope recall: 15%, 5%, 0%.
limits: Same limits. Two examples only for the qualitative claims.
agent_relevance: Different theories catch different fallacies. A rule check and a scheme check may complement each other.

source: Zhou et al. (2025), same paper: what the PD prompt asks the model to do
finding: The PD prompt lists the 10 rules with violation criteria. For each statement the model names the most significant violated rules, then maps to one of six fallacy labels. It acts as a structured chain of thought built on the rules.
numbers: Prompt contents: instruction, task, 10 rules with definitions and violation criteria. Model Qwen-3 8B with reasoning on.
limits: Prompt text not fully read. The mapping from rules to six labels is lossy, as the authors admit.
agent_relevance: Rule-first reasoning is cheap to copy as a guardrail check, but it needs a test on matched valid items before it is trusted.

source: Goffredo, Haddadan, Vorakitphan, Cabrio and Villata (2022) Fallacious Argument Classification in Political Debates (IJCAI-22)
finding: Defines fallacies, in the pragma-dialectical sense, as speech acts that violate the rules of a rational discussion for assumed persuasive gain, and annotates six types in US presidential debates 1960 to 2016. This is the source dataset (ElecDeb60To16-fallacy) later used in LLM studies.
numbers: 31 debates; 1,628 annotated spans: Appeal to Emotion 1,016, Appeal to Authority 234, Ad Hominem 188, False Cause 69, Slogans 64, Slippery Slope 57. Agreement among 3 annotators on 9 sections: Krippendorff alpha 0.46 to 0.60 (Ad Hominem 0.53, Authority 0.58, Emotion 0.46, Slogans 0.60).
limits: Only moderate agreement, so labels are noisy. Class imbalance is large (62% emotion). The authors say the task stays unsolved. The 'speech acts that violate the rules' wording is quoted from Zhou et al., who cite Goffredo.
agent_relevance: Gold labels for 'rule-violating' moves are themselves uncertain. A scaffold that uses such labels as ground truth inherits that noise.

source: Goffredo et al. (2022), same paper: classifier results
finding: A Longformer with 4,096-token speech context and a joint loss reached macro F1 0.61 on six main categories without argument features. Adding argument component and relation labels raised it to 0.84. Fourteen sub-categories gave macro F1 0.42.
numbers: BERT 0.55, RoBERTa 0.53, Longformer 0.57, Longformer joint loss 0.61, Transformer-XL 0.47 to 0.53. With component+relation labels: precision 0.84, recall 0.85, macro F1 0.84, accuracy 0.89. Average of three runs. Ablation F1 without features: Ad Hominem 0.56, False Cause 0.43, Slippery Slope 0.50.
limits: Gold argument labels are given at test time, which inflates the gain. Fine-tuned, not zero-shot. Errors come from Slogans, Appeal to Emotion and Ad Hominem sharing vocabulary.
agent_relevance: Structure (claim, premise, support or attack) helps a lot when it is known. A scaffold that maps argument structure first may help later checks.

source: Jin et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection (Findings of EMNLP)
finding: Introduces the logical fallacy detection task with datasets LOGIC and LOGICCLIMATE. Twelve pretrained language models did poorly. A structure-aware classifier that masks repeated spans beat the best of them.
numbers: LOGIC: 2,449 samples, 13 fallacy types (faulty generalization 18.01%, ad hominem 12.33%). LOGICCLIMATE: 1,109 climate claims. Pretrained model micro F1 8.62% to 53.31%. Structure-aware model +5.46% on LOGIC and +4.51% on LOGICCLIMATE over the best.
limits: Data come from online quiz sites, so examples are clean and textbook-like. Models are old (2022). Not a pragma-dialectical test; cites van Eemeren only as background.
agent_relevance: Textbook-style fallacy labels are a poor test of real reasoning. Use only as a weak baseline.

source: Helwe, Calamai, Paris, Clavel and Suchanek (2024) MAFALDA: Benchmark and Comprehensive Study of Fallacy Detection and Classification
finding: Unifies earlier datasets under one taxonomy and tests models zero-shot against human annotators. Models are weak, and the task is hard for people too.
numbers: F1 level 0 (fallacy or not) / level 1 / level 2: GPT-3.5 175B 0.627 / 0.201 / 0.138; Vicuna 13B 0.557 / 0.173 / 0.100; Zephyr 7B 0.524 / 0.192 / 0.098; Mistral Instruct 7B 0.536 / 0.144 / 0.069. Average human on 20 samples: 0.749 / 0.352 / 0.186.
limits: Human study uses only 20 examples and 4 annotators. Old open models and GPT-3.5. Subjective task with low agreement.
agent_relevance: Fine-grained fallacy naming is unreliable even for people. Binary 'is this flawed' is more reliable than naming the type.

source: Pan, Wu, Li and Luu (2024) Are LLMs Good Zero-Shot Fallacy Classifiers? (EMNLP)
finding: Zero-shot prompting of LLMs (single-round and multi-round with extraction, summarisation, chain-of-thought) gives acceptable fallacy classification, beats full-shot fine-tuned baselines in all out-of-distribution settings, and multi-round prompting helps small models most.
numbers: Numbers not recorded; only abstract and introduction read. Cites van Eemeren et al. (2009) as background for the fallacy concept.
limits: No numbers taken. No use of pragma-dialectical rules.
agent_relevance: Prompt structure matters more for small models. Suggests a staged check helps a small agent.

source: Jeong, Jang and Park (2025) LLMs Are Better Logical Fallacy Reasoners with Counterargument, Explanation, and Goal-Aware Prompt Formulation
finding: Adds a generated counterargument, explanation and goal to each text, queries validity, and ranks queries by model confidence. Improves fallacy detection in zero-shot and fine-tuned use.
numbers: 5 domains, 29 fallacy types, GPT and LLaMA models. F1 gains up to 0.60 zero-shot and up to 0.45 fine-tuned.
limits: Only the abstract was read. Gains are against weak baselines. No pragma-dialectical framing.
agent_relevance: Generating the counter-case before judging is a cheap check that parallels the antagonist role in a critical discussion.

source: Mouchel et al. (2025) A Logical Fallacy-Informed Framework for Argument Generation (FIPO)
finding: Preference training with a fallacy-type classification loss cuts fallacies in generated arguments. Human evaluation favours it over baselines. It does not use the pragma-dialectical rules.
numbers: Fallacy rate reduced by up to 17.5%; SFT baseline about 34%; FIPO fallacy rate 17% and win rate 63.5% (GPT-4 judged, Llama-2 base). Authors classified 200 arguments themselves to check GPT-4 labels.
limits: Training method, not a scaffold. Partly judged by GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Fallacy awareness can be trained. Our agent does not train, so only the idea of a fallacy label per output carries over.

source: Singh, Pathak and Singh (2026) Fallacy Benchmarks Measure Scheme Recognition, Not Fallacy Detection
finding: Fallacy detectors learn which argumentation scheme a text uses, not whether it uses it correctly. When correct arguments with the same scheme are built, detectors flag them as fallacies. The same pattern appears in three zero-shot LLMs.
numbers: Wrong-scheme negatives are labeled as their real scheme 85.9% of the time and as the source fallacy 0.4%. A model scoring 16.6% false positives on CoCoLoFa's own valid class flags 58.9% of the scheme-matched negatives. Scheme Foils: 655 matched and 738 wrong-scheme CoCoLoFa items, 387 and 389 Reddit items. Zero-shot models: Claude Sonnet 5, Haiku 4.5, Qwen3.6-27B.
limits: Preprint, v2. Items are LLM-generated and filtered; 3 annotators judged 72 matched negatives. Uses Walton schemes, not the PD rules.
agent_relevance: Strong warning: an LLM rule checker will over-flag sound arguments that merely look like a fallacy. Test any check on matched valid cases.

source: Singh et al. (2026), same paper: where detector errors go
finding: Fallacy benchmarks pair fallacy classes with a 'none' class that holds everything not labeled a fallacy. When the detector misses a fallacy, the error lands on 'none', not on another fallacy type.
numbers: Fine-tuned ModernBERT on CoCoLoFa: about 76% of misclassified fallacy items go to the valid class (last digit cut in the text I read).
limits: Exact figure truncated; treat as about three quarters.
agent_relevance: Missed detection, not mislabeling, is the main error. A scaffold needs a positive test for soundness, not only a hunt for flaws.

source: Chen, Greschner, Klinger, Klenk and Eger (2026) Emotionally Charged, Logically Blurred
finding: LLM-added emotional framing lowers human fallacy detection. Fear, sadness and enjoyment framings also raise convincingness.
numbers: Human fallacy-detection F1 down 14.5% on average with emotional framing. Share of arguments labeled fallacious fell from 91% to 86%. Eight LLMs benchmarked on injecting emotion; 1,000 arguments for the human study; Prolific raters. Only 2 of 20 double-annotated items differed.
limits: Preprint. Crowd raters. Mentions pragma-dialectics only in passing.
agent_relevance: Emotional framing is a presentational device in strategic-maneuvering terms and hides rule violations from human readers. An agent should strip framing before judging.

source: Gajewska, Budzynska and Chudziak (2026) Benchmarking Argumentative Behaviour of LLMs: Defences Against Character Attacks
finding: Five LLMs answered real ad hominem attacks from US debates. Humans rebut logically 59%, counterattack on character 32%, use undercutters 9%. LLMs mostly rebut (67 to 76%) and rarely counterattack. Models often treat an ad hominem as a toxic trigger.
numbers: N = 97 exchanges from ElecDeb60To16-fallacy. Human-vs-LLM annotator agreement: Cohen kappa 0.62 (GPT 5.1) and 0.63 (Grok 4.1 reasoning). Only Gemini 3 Pro and Grok 4.1 reasoning used the ethotic layer. Based on Walton and Budzynska dialogue games, not PD.
limits: Preprint. Small N. Per-model table did not survive text extraction, so only the prose figures are recorded.
agent_relevance: Rule-governed dialogue games could regulate the agent's action space. Safety tuning may block legitimate moves, so rule checks should not depend on tone.

source: SEP (2024) Fallacies; sections 4.2 and 4.4 on why fallacies seem good and links to bias
finding: Psychology is excluded from the pragma-dialectical definition, but other authors link specific biases to specific fallacies (Correia 2011) and give cognitive and rhetorical reasons why bad arguments look good (Oswald and Herman 2020; Hansen 2023). Thagard (2011) says motivated inference needs something closer to psychotherapy than informal logic.
numbers: No numbers. Hitchcock (2023) found little improvement in how six textbooks treat fallacies.
limits: Review text only.
agent_relevance: Pragma-dialectics gives no account of why a model slips into fallacies. For that, use the bias and debiasing work done in parallel subfields.

source: Searches for pragma-dialectical LLM work: arXiv full-text search (several queries, 2026-11-17)
finding: A query on pragma-dialectical or pragma-dialectics returned one relevant arXiv paper (Zhou et al. 2025). Papers on fallacies, ad hominem and dialogue games exist but mostly use Walton schemes or fallacy taxonomies, not the ten rules. No study tested whether pragma-dialectical rules improve LLM reasoning in a controlled way.
numbers: 1 relevant hit among about 5 pragma-dialectics queries. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited; WebSearch budget exhausted. Coverage is therefore incomplete.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search. Journal work in Argumentation and ISSA proceedings is not indexed on arXiv and was not reachable.
agent_relevance: The subfield is thin for our purpose. Keep it background only, as planned.
